segments.text: Let's start with a simple scenario.
A high school student wants to know if listening to their Spotify height playlist will help
them focus on chemistry, or if it will just be a distraction.
So they ask an AI.
This image shows the AI's response to that prompt, and it looks incredibly helpful.
It cites a 2022 Stanford study of 1200 high school students, noting that familiar instrumental
music improved recall by 18%, provided the volume stayed below 60 decibels.
The study does not exist.
The reason this is so easy to fall for is that every specific detail sounds perfectly credible.
Stanford is a real university.
The sample size of 1,200 students feels robust.
18% is a precise measured result.
And keeping the volume under 60 decibels sounds like genuine careful advice.
All of these elements make the answer easier to trust.
Yet, if you search for this data, you will find no published paper, no research team, and
no original source material to open.
A hallucination is a factual claim AI makes up that sounds true but isn't.
These errors can be incredibly difficult to spot because the AI rarely invents an entire
answer out of thin air.
Instead, it weaves completely fake findings into a paragraph containing facts that are
real.
This infographic outlines exactly why these confident research sounding errors happen.
First, AI learns its language patterns from massive databases of human-written text.
That source material inherently includes human mistakes, jokes, and lies,
all of which shape the patterns the model absorbs.
Second, when it generates a response, it builds its sentences one token at a time.
It continuously calculates which word is mathematically most likely to come next,
based on those learned patterns.
patterns. Because AI is explicitly trained to be helpful to the user, it rarely stops
to admit it lacks information. It simply keeps trying to answer. Probable does not equal true.
At its core, the system is a pattern matching machine. A highly probable sequence of words
can sound perfectly accurate and authoritative, even if the underlying claim it is making
is entirely fabricated. Fabricating data is one type of hallucination, but AI can also
fail by misinterpreting real information.
Consider what happened when a user asked a search engine how to keep cheese from sliding
off a slice of pizza.
The AI confidently suggested mixing about 1-8th of a cup of non-toxic glue directly into
the pizza sauce.
This flowchart breaks down where that bizarre answer came from.
It traced back to an old joke on Reddit written in the style of sincere cooking advice.
The AI successfully found real text online, but it completely missed the semantic meaning
behind it, processing a sarcastic comment into strict culinary instruction. The
Reddit comment was real. The cooking advice was not. Because hallucinations
sound identical to accurate answers, you will not catch everyone. The skill you
need is paying close attention, and noticing when a specific detail or piece
of advice just doesn't add up. When you spot a detail that feels off, use this
three-step framework shown here to verify the claim. The process moves in a strict
sequence. Notice the claim, find the original source, and check the match to see if the source
actually supports what the AI said. Let's apply this to the Stanford example. First,
notice the claim. The specific details we need to verify are the existence of a 2022 study of 1200
students and the 18% improvement in recall. Second, find the source. You need to look for
original study itself, rather than accepting a prestigious university's name as proof.
Third, check the match. Since there is no original study supporting those specific
numbers, they cannot be repeated as facts. Failing to find a source does not instantly
prove a claim is false, but it does mean the claim remains entirely unverified.
Now, let's apply the framework to the pizza example. First, notice the claim.
claim. The core assertion here is that glue belongs in pizza sauce.
Second, find the source. In this case, tracking down the real Reddit comment successfully
completes the second step. Third, check the match. When we check the context of that source,
we see it was a joke. It fails the match check because it doesn't support the literal advice.
Finding real text is not enough. It must support the claim being made. Verification
requires two conditions to be met.
The source document must actually exist,
and the AI's interpretation of that document
must be strictly accurate.
This graphic summarizes the final rule
for handling AI outputs.
Hallucinations sound like every other AI answer.
When something doesn't add up, trace the claim to its source.
